purpose: Record independently researched Genoese/Venetian presence around the Black Sea and distinguish political possession, concession, colony, merchant access, and trade-network evidence for the 1326 scenario.

method.rule: Do not convert merchant presence or trade access into political ownership.
method.dateRule: Evidence after 1326-04-07 is not projected backward into the scenario start.
method.geometryRule: No canonical polygon is promoted from this review; sites are spatial anchors and status evidence only.
method.conflictRule: Later summaries that date colonies after 1326 are preferred over generic statements that merely describe a site's later Genoese importance.

findings: Byzantine agreements in 1267 and 1303 recognized a substantial Genoese settlement area at Galata/Pera with houses, warehouses, commercial privileges and autonomous legal/administrative arrangements.
The major masonry fortification phase should not be back-projected wholesale: Treccani dates a true enclosing wall to 1335 and later expansion to 1348.
For 1326, represent Galata as a Genoese commercial/urban enclave with a distinct footprint, not as an independent sovereign province.
Benedetto Zaccaria seized Chios in 1304 and received it as a Byzantine concession; later Zaccaria rule continued until Byzantine reconquest in 1329.
Therefore Chios is a high-confidence 1326 Genoese-family political possession, but not simply a polygon labelled Republic of Genoa.
The island's mastich production and maritime position make it both a political anchor and an economic-network anchor.
The Zaccaria/Cattaneo family held Phocaea and its alum interests during the years immediately preceding 1326.
Treccani records Cattaneo as lord of Phocaea from 1314 and notes an annual tribute arrangement with Saruhan for security of alum transport.
Andronikos III recovered the Genoese possessions in 1329, so the 1329 recovery must not be projected into the 1326 start state.
Martino Zaccaria controlled the port fortifications of Smyrna before their later loss to the Turkish/Aydinid side.
Because the exact lower-port/upper-city configuration is spatially complex, this review treats the port fortification as an anchor rather than assigning the whole city to Genoa.
The later 1329 changes are explicitly excluded from the 1326 snapshot.
Genoese merchants had an established presence at Trebizond by the late 13th/early 14th century and a consul is attested before 1290 in the Trebizond trade framework.
Venice received a formal chrysobull in 1319 granting land at Leontokastron for a fondaco and freedom of trade subject to customs and weighing taxes.
These are merchant-community and commercial-privilege anchors, not evidence that Genoa or Venice owned the city or its surrounding territory.
Genoese access to Caffa followed the 13th-century Byzantine-Genoese settlement framework; after the 1307 crisis, Genoese dominion in Crimea and Tana was re-established in 1313.
Caffa functioned as a major Genoese administrative and commercial center for the northern Black Sea network.
The 1326 map should represent Caffa as a Genoese colonial/trading node, not as evidence for Genoese control of the whole Crimean peninsula.

siteReviews.scenarioStatus: present-as-trade-node; exact political status requires further source review
findings: Soldaia/Sudak appears in the established Genoese Black Sea network, while Venetian commercial activity was also present in the region.
The evidence currently supports a trade-network node more securely than a single 1326 sovereign-control polygon.
Further charter and archaeological review is required before assigning a political owner.
Genoese dominion in La Tana/Azaq was re-established in 1313, while Venetian trade was also active there during the late medieval period.
The site should be represented as a commercial node with competing Latin communities rather than a generic Venetian or Genoese territorial polygon without further date-specific charter evidence.
UNESCO tentative-list material describes later Genoese and Venetian activity at Sinop and a Genoese flag on the 1351 Laurentiana map.
Kate Fleet's chronological review, as summarized by Oxford Academic, argues that the Genoese settlements at Sinop and Amasra were established between 1360 and 1380.
Therefore a 1326 Genoese colony at Sinop must not be inserted merely because Sinop became a major Genoese center later.
Sinop remains a high-value port and political-control anchor for the Candaroğlu state, but Latin colony status is deferred.

Generic heritage summaries describe Amasra as a Genoese colony, but a chronological review of contemporary-source evidence places the establishment of the Genoese settlements at Amasra and Sinop between 1360 and 1380.
Therefore the later Genoese-colony label cannot be projected backward to 7 April 1326.
Amasra remains an important Black Sea port anchor whose later Genoese phase is retained as future temporal evidence.

modelRules: Genoese family lordship is distinct from Republic of Genoa sovereign territory.
A merchant quarter/fondaco is distinct from political ownership of its host city.
A trade route or commercial privilege is not a territorial claim.
Later colony dates are not projected backward into 1326.
City, port, fortress, quarter and hinterland must be separately modelled where the evidence supports different authorities.
These records are evidence-only and cannot promote canonical political geometry without independent geometry reconstruction and temporal review.
